page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Palindromic sequence defined
steps.margin_note: The full definition with the direction condition. Three lines.
lines: A PALINDROME in DNA is a sequence of base pairs
that reads the SAME on both strands, when both
are read in the same 5' to 3' direction.
steps.why: Reading both strands in the same direction is what makes them identical; read the other way they are complements, not palindromes.
common_mistakes: Saying it reads the same backwards. That is a word palindrome; a DNA palindrome is about TWO strands.
Leaving out the 5' to 3' condition. Without it the definition is wrong.
steps.memory_tip: Same reading on both strands, both read the same way round.

steps.label: An example
steps.margin_note: Both strands, then the check spelled out. This is what earns the mark.

lines.text: 5'-GAATTC-3' reads the same on both strands

lines: 5'  G A A T T C  3'
3'  C T T A A G  5'
Read the lower strand 5' to 3' — that is, right
to left — and it also reads GAATTC.
steps.why: Writing both strands out is the only way to show the property, because it is a relationship between two strands rather than a feature of one.
common_mistakes: Giving a single strand. A palindrome needs BOTH strands written.
Giving no example at all. The example is half the answer.
steps.memory_tip: Write both strands and read the bottom one backwards.
